transcript.text: We replaced our old condenser dryer with a heat pump one about a month ago and honestly it's driving me mad, a normal load of towels takes nearly 3 and a half hours, the old one did it in about 90 minutes. It also feels barely warm for the first half hour when I open the door to check. Surely that's not right? Is it faulty?

It is very likely not faulty. Heat-pump dryers work like a fridge in reverse: they dry at a much lower temperature to save energy, which means the drum feels only warm (not hot) and cycles take significantly longer than old vented or condenser models. A 3-hour cycle for towels is actually quite normal for this technology. However, performance can drop if airflow is restricted. Please check that the lint filter in the door and the condenser unit at the bottom are clean of fluff, and ensure you aren't accidentally using a low-heat or eco programme.

Ok well I do clean the fluff filters after every load, and the one at the bottom I did about two weeks ago and it looked clean. I'm using Cotton Cupboard Dry with a full load. It's in the garage and it's pretty cold out there, if that matters?

That cold garage environment is very likely the main factor here. Heat-pump dryers extract moisture from the air in the drum; if the surrounding room is cold, the machine has to work much harder and longer to maintain its internal drying temperature. This explains why it feels barely warm for a long time and takes nearly 3½ hours. Could you please check that condenser unit again right now? If it’s blocked, it will significantly worsen drying times even in a cold room. Also, to help me confirm if this is typical for your specific machine, could you tell me the make and model number?
[Helpful to see: image "Where the condenser and water tank are" — On a condenser dryer the water container pulls out at the top and the condenser/heat exchanger sits behind a flap at the bottom front — slide it out and rinse it. Condenser/heat-pump dryers only; layout may differ.]
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
It's a Bosch, model WTH85223GB, it's on the receipt. I only cleaned the bottom filter two weeks ago and it looked clean then, so do I really need to pull it out again?

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. You don't need to pull it out again if it was truly clean two weeks ago, but condenser units on heat-pump dryers (like your Bosch WTH85223GB) can clog with fine fluff very quickly, and a partially blocked unit forces the machine to run much longer. However, to rule out a simple restriction, please take the condenser unit (usually behind the bottom flap) out now and rinse it under a tap; if water runs straight through without resistance, it's clean. If you find it is clean, then the long cycle time is normal for your conditions.

Ok, I'll pull it out and rinse it if I really have to. I did that two weeks ago though and it was fine. And if it's clean, you're saying 3 and a half hours is just normal for it in the garage? The time left on the display keeps jumping up too, is that ok?

Yes, 3½ hours is completely normal for a heat-pump dryer in a cold garage. The machine has to work much harder to extract moisture when the surrounding air is chilly, which extends the cycle time significantly compared to your old condenser model. Regarding the display jumping around: this is also normal behaviour. Heat-pump dryers use sensors to estimate how long is left based on current humidity and temperature; if the load shifts or the room is cold, that estimate changes rapidly. It does not indicate a fault.

candidates: Blocked filters or condenser restricting airflow (medium)
Incorrect programme selection (e.g. low-heat or eco mode) (low)
